text.text:
My experience at Mojo Latin Restaurant was overall very good, and I would definitely recommend this place if you enjoy a vibrant atmosphere and flavorful Latin food. From the moment we walked in, the environment stood out immediately. The restaurant has a lively, stylish, and welcoming ambiance that makes it a great place to go with friends, family, or even for a casual date night. The music, decoration, and overall energy create a really enjoyable dining experience.

The food was delicious. We tried several dishes, and most of them were excellent. The Peruvian ceviche tasted very good and fresh, although as a Peruvian, I have to say it was not exactly an authentic traditional Peruvian ceviche. Still, the flavor was enjoyable and well prepared. The lomo saltado was really good, probably one of my favorite dishes of the night. The meat was flavorful, well cooked, and combined perfectly with the fries and rice. We also ordered empanadas and guac with chips, and both were excellent. The guacamole tasted fresh, and the chips were crispy and perfectly paired with it.

The waitresses were almost perfect: attentive, friendly, and professional during most of the experience. However, there was one detail that I believe the restaurant should improve. The gratuity was already included in the receipt, but we still felt pushed to add an extra tip. That is something that should be avoided. Customers should never feel pressured to leave additional tips beyond the gratuity already added. If customers truly feel happy with the service, they will naturally choose to leave more.

Besides that issue, I genuinely enjoyed the restaurant. Great food, amazing atmosphere, and a very enjoyable experience overall. I would return again and recommend it to others looking for a fun Latin restaurant in Forest Hills.

editorialSummary.text: Casual cantina serving up refined Mexican classics & cocktails amid concrete floors & mod seating.

text.text:
Casa Enrique is good, but has dropped off a bit in terms of creative spark and meticulous service.

Most of what we ordered was tasty. It’s comforting and accessible, but it stops short of being truly outstanding or memorable. The Rajas con Crema gets an honorable mention for being the least liked and eaten dish. It felt like an afterthought in preparation, presentation, and flavor (on paper sounds delicious but in person it was like a bunch of random ingredients thrown together with no seasoning. It could be so much better if refined and tweaked).

While the portions were appropriate, our server could have guided us through the menu more efficiently (like not letting us order so much rice but silver lining more leftovers).

It’s a solid 3.5 star experience, but I wouldn't rush back or say it’s worth crossing boroughs for ($18 guac, $20 cocktails). This kitchen plays it very safe and unfortunately makes for a static meal. I hope they consider taking bigger risks with unique ingredients and bolder flavor profiles/textures.

My friends and I were excited to finally try Casa Enrique after hearing so much about it and seeing it recognized in the Michelin Guide. Unfortunately, the experience didn’t quite live up to our expectations.

The food was good, but nothing really stood out as memorable. I ordered the pork shoulder special, which I enjoyed, but it wasn’t a dish that would make me rush back. One of my friends ordered a soup dish and was particularly disappointed with it.

The atmosphere was probably the biggest challenge for us. We were seated in a corner at the end of the dining room, and despite the restaurant not being especially crowded, the music was very loud. It was difficult to have a conversation at our table and even hard to hear the staff at times. The seating also felt quite tight, and we noticed the guests seated next to us struggling to get in and out of their seats comfortably.

Service was another area that could be improved. While I didn’t personally have any major issues, several people in our group felt that some interactions came across as rushed and somewhat unfriendly, as if the staff were exhausted and didn’t really want to be there.

Overall, the meal was decent, but given the reputation and expectations surrounding the restaurant, we left feeling underwhelmed. It’s not a bad restaurant by any means, but it didn’t deliver the experience we were hoping for.

Leaving 5 stars because I have loved coming to this place regularly for the past 2 years, but I'd like to leave honest feedback for the new ownership.

Took my friend for his birthday dinner in mid-March and they were out of many of their wines by the bottle, but was told it was because they had new management and the list was changing. Also saw they had changed their fries and was disappointed about that. I figured I'd give them some time to iron out the kinks with their transition and went back for the first time since then last Sunday and was very disappointed.

They were out of several kinds of oysters and snow crab claws when we tried to order. We were offered bread that never arrived, and the deviled eggs that we regularly ordered were thoughtlessly prepared and didn't come with as much lobster as usual. I really enjoyed the new scallop dish and it was nice to see our regular shucker, but those were the only positives of the experience.

The host stand was mobbed when we arrived with no host in sight, so we ended up seating ourselves at the bar after waiting almost ten minutes. The lighting was blindingly bright and music was so quiet that I could only tell it was playing when I went to the bathroom. You can tell from the menus that whoever is updating them doesn't care about matching font sizes or spelling things correctly, and their wine by the bottle list had still not been updated after 2 months.

I noticed that some prices had lowered which was appreciated, but if it comes with this drop in quality, I would happily pay more. I will continue to give this place more chances because it is the only restaurant in the area that is seafood focused with a raw bar, but I hope that the new ownership takes these notes into consideration. I want to see this neighborhood institution succeed!

So this is after my second visit here, both times during weekdays.

First off, the price here is very cheap. You can chug a Blue Label on a rock for only $30 a pop. For reference to whiskey lovers, they used to be $40~$50 a glass back in ~2020 in the city.

I'm an Izakaya-goer, particularly for the ones in NYC as I rarely go to any venues in Flushing but this place is on par, if not better than some places around midtown.

The quality of food is what you can expect from an Izakaya standard, especially for its low price point. It's technically a sake bar with some small portion dishes to fill you up with.

You're not paying for Cote or Howoo KBBQ quality, let's be real.

The atmosphere, I love the oriental yet contemporary touch they have for the rooms and the hallway, particularly the bar.

And speaking of the bar, the attentiveness of the staff can be pretty inconsistent at the bar. I had some few trouble getting someone to take additional orders or close out my tab as I wasn't just hollering at a random staff,  considering they're probably all assigned to certain tables.

Overall, a bit mixed experience between 2 visits so far but props to Wei at the bar for making the first visit smooth. The bartender was literally grilling, serving, making cocktails and closing out tabs like a one-man brigade.

P.S. Like some other reviews have mentioned, their suggested tip calculates from the total with tax applied, not a deal breaker but kind of leaves a bit of bad taste.

I would've given this place one star if it weren't for the service. Overall, the food was mediocre and pretty underwhelming.

We started with the bone marrow, which was disappointing. It had an oddly fishy taste when it should've been rich and buttery. It also lacked proper seasoning, so we ended up sending it back.

For the entree, we ordered the dry aged porterhouse, priced at nearly $200. We asked for medium, but it came out well done, which was a letdown. The chimichurri didn't taste authentic, and while the signature steak sauce was fine, it wasn't anything memorable. We also ordered a side of bacon, which was decent but I've had better. The chili prawn noodles were another miss. It came with only four shrimp, wasn't spicy at all, and used spaghetti noodles, which felt off for the dish.

The only real highlights were the creamed spinach and shishito peppers. Those were solid and you just can't go wrong with it.

At best, I'd recommend coming here for the cocktails and the view. The food alone doesn't justify it.

I added an extra star strictly because of the service. Shirley was excellent. She was knowledgeable, attentive, and gave great wine recommendations. Very accommodating and genuinely pleasant, which made the experience better overall.

Jiang Nan is a Chinese Fusion restaurant that aims to offer an indulgent and comforting dining experience. Their menu includes traditional entrees (such as Peking Duck, Xiao Long Bao, and Grill Fish), seasonal menus with trending ingredients, and creative drink menus. While a bit on the pricey side, I do think it is worth the cost.

The Stir-fried Shredded Cabbage w. Pork Belly was different than expected. The cabbage was not as crispy as I hoped, but was still delicious. Surprisingly, the pork belly was shredded, rather than the usual thinly sliced. Nonetheless, this dish was delicious and I highly recommend it.

Another highly recommended dish is the Kimchi & Cheese Fried Rice. Delivered in a wooden barrel, there was a perfect mixture of kimchi and cheese. After mixing them, you get an even balance of both flavors and it retains its light touch.

I would also recommend the Braised Beef Flank w. Potato! The beef flank and potatoes were super soft and tender. The chef's special marination was heavenly. I rarely leave negative reviews, but our recent meal was disappointing for our table of 5. Judging by the quality and presentation of the food the focus here is for the kitchen to quickly clear orders.

The Baked Clams for $34 were unfortunately mushy, consisting of wet - rather than being properly toasted - breadcrumbs in a pool of butter and garlic.

The $31 house salad was bland, featuring entirely flavorless olives. How does that happen?

The Chicken Scarpariello ($40), like other reviewers have mentioned was dry from either sitting out and reheating or just overcooked. Either or it was not good. We left a lot of that on the table.

The Filet of Sole had zero flavor. That was the consensus from everyone at the table. We left it unfinished. Not worth $46.

The pasta with meat sauce was like no other I've ever had. The meat was overcooked and hard which made for a strange bite.

The Shrimp Lucciano was good but nothing exceptional. Lots of butter, onions, and a splash of wine. Absolutuely not worth $49.

The Calamari in marinara was good.
